The Gregorian calendar is the solar calendar adopted by the Catholic Church in 1582 and gradually adopted worldwide as the standard civil calendar. Designed by Pope Gregory XIII to correct accumulated drift in the Julian calendar, it rules most international timekeeping today and anchors the Western new year on January first.

The Gregorian calendar reformed the Julian calendar, which had drifted ten days out of alignment with the solar year by the sixteenth century due to an overestimated leap-year rule. The fix was to omit leap years in century years—1700, 1800, 1900—unless divisible by four hundred. This was a more accurate correction than the Julian system's simple every-four-years rule. It was adopted first by Catholic nations including Spain, Portugal, and Italy, and slowly by Protestant and Orthodox regions. Britain and its colonies, including America, adopted it in 1752.

The Gregorian calendar imposes a fixed solar year of approximately 365.24219 days, enabling precise long-term calendars without the month-drift inherent in purely lunar systems. The leap-year exception—every four hundred years, not one hundred—means the Gregorian year drifts only one day per approximately three thousand three hundred years, an extraordinarily accurate long-term system. Adoption was politically fraught, with Orthodox and some Protestant churches resisting what they saw as papal authority, delaying synchronization into the twentieth century for some regions.

The ten-day jump in October 1582, when October fourth was followed by October fifteenth, sparked urban legends of the "lost ten days" and briefly confused merchants and clergy worldwide. France, Spain, and Portugal adopted it immediately, while Russia and Greece held out until the twentieth century. Some Orthodox communities use the Julian calendar still for religious purposes. The Gregorian calendar coexists with religious and cultural calendars including Islamic, Hebrew, Chinese, and Hindu traditions, but dominates international commerce, law, and science.
